author: simulation_agent

numbers.name: bead_diameter
numbers.note: the tracer the question is about, measured directly by the operator on 2026-09-19 with a coefficient of variation no greater than 2 per cent. Cited as kb: rather than calibration: -- the grade is E2 either way, but this agent holds no calibration and the citation is what puts the entry in kb_refs

numbers.name: diffusivity
numbers.note: bulk Stokes-Einstein: sphere, bulk, no slip. Those assumptions stay in the value. The relation is the librarian's (kb:tracer_diffusivity_expected), not a second one -- recomputing a quantity the store holds is a detour, and citing it is what gets the one name. This is the expectation the run is checked against, and the engine derives its own from the same bath rather than being handed this number

numbers.name: tau_d
numbers.note: kb:tau_d. The grade follows the inputs, not the entry: a formula applied to estimates yields an estimate

numbers.name: dt_resolution_factor
numbers.note: how far below the diffusive time the step must sit: two decades

numbers.name: integration_timestep_max
numbers.note: upper bound only; nothing in A1 bounds the step from below

assumptions.statement: Two decades below the shortest resolved time is the usual margin for an overdamped integrator, but it is a convention rather than a derivation: no convergence scan on this model has been run.
assumptions.falsifier: a timestep scan showing the diffusivity flat over a wider range of steps replaces this factor with a measured one

assumptions.statement: The tracers do not interact. No pair potential is part of this configuration and none is declared in capabilities/simulation.json, so the diffusive time is the shortest time in the system. This premise is what the bound rests on: with interactions the curvature time of the potential, gamma over k, is usually far shorter, and a step set from the diffusive time would be wrong by decades rather than by a factor.
assumptions.falsifier: any interaction parameter entering the model retires this bound and the axis has to be re-run against the curvature time

kb_refs.claim: The diffusive time is the time a sphere needs to diffuse its own diameter, and it sets the shortest record length from which a mean squared displacement can be read.
The particles in the bottle in use have a diameter of 5 micrometres, with a coefficient of variation no greater than 2 per cent, measured directly by the operator on 2026-09-19.

note: The form of the bound is the librarian's definition and its prefactor is an estimate, so S4 should weight it accordingly (4.5.2). The premise that matters most is not a number at all: the tracers do not interact, and a_non_interacting records it.
